newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends lower as mark gains on French election jitters.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends lower as mark gains on French election jitters.

text.p: NEW YORK, May 28 - The dollar fell broadly Wednesday as mounting uncertainty ahead of runoff elections in France strengthened the German mark and anticipation of higher interest rates in Japan boosted the yen.

The mark also gained against a variety of European currencies, surging briefly to its highest level in four-months versus the French franc. Traders reported that central banks of Spain and Sweden intervened to support their respective currencies against the mark.

Rumours circulated in foreign exchange markets that a privately conducted poll showed the French socialist party could win a clear majority in the final round of parliamentary elections Sunday. The socialists favour a less stringent interpretation of the criteria that countries must meet to qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union, or EMU. By contrast, German officials have emphasised the need for strict adherence to the standards for inclusion in the single European currency.
"There's going to be a lot of infighting. Chances are greater for an EMU delay and so the mark strengthens," said Chris Turner, a research director at I.D.E.A. Inc., a consultancy firm.
Doubts about plans for the single European currency, scheduled for debut on January 1, 1999, often boosts the mark, which is viewed as a safe haven currency in Europe.
In late New York trading Wednesday, the dollar fetched 1.6956 marks, down from 1.7055 marks on Tuesday. The dollar fell to 115.85 Japanese yen from 116.67 yen.
The dollar slid to 1.4111 Swiss francs from 1.4205 Swiss francs, but was unchanged at Canadian $1.3828. The British pound rose to $1.6393 from $1.6311.

Tension surrounding the proposed single European currency intensified later in the day. Germany's Bundesbank issued a statement rejecting a plan by the German government to revalue the bank's gold and currency reserves to help cover a shortfall in budget revenues that would aid Germany's efforts to qualify for the single European currency. The German central bank warned Wednesday the plan ran the risk of undermining the stability of the single European currency. The German government, however, said it would go ahead with its plans.
Initially, the dollar erased its losses against the mark after the central bank statement was released but it later gave back these gains.

The response to the central bank announcement was "perverse", said Kevin Harris, an international economist at MCM CurrencyWatch because it implied a delay in the start of European Economic and Monetary Union, a development that should have supported the mark.
But the market appeared to have anticipated the statement and traders took profits on the announcement, he said.
In Asian trading, the yield on the 10-year Japanese government bond rose as high as 2.7 percent on Wednesday, up from 2.645 percent Tuesday.
"The one thing really pushing the yen higher is the perception of higher rates in Japan," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Sakura Bank Ltd in New York.
Yet Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita told a news conference Wednesday that monetary policy will continue to emphasise strengthening the basis of the economic recovery.
The Japanese central bank has kept its official interest rates at record low levels to help stimulate economic growth.
